# Mathematical statements and complete proofs

These derivations restate and expand the supplied SAGE author manuscript. Equations are displayed as scalable vector images; the [complete editable LaTeX source](sources/THEORY.md.in) and a [notation and viewing guide](MATH_RENDERING.md) are provided. They are mathematical proofs under stated hypotheses; the supplied floating-point artifacts do not independently establish the interval hypotheses.

## 1. Domain and regularity

Let <img src="assets/math/inline-2499aeb5140d9bd3.svg" width="60" height="15" alt="D\subset\mathbb R^n"> be compact with <img src="assets/math/inline-9a2df1b5954d33ea.svg" width="69" height="15" alt="0\in\operatorname{int}D">, and let the closed-loop vector field <img src="assets/math/inline-3e507e9542909164.svg" width="19" height="18" alt="f_\kappa"> be locally Lipschitz on an open neighborhood of <img src="assets/math/inline-2b08ffd953f7c889.svg" width="17" height="14" alt="D">, with <img src="assets/math/inline-0e9cbfc3e569bae4.svg" width="72" height="19" alt="f_\kappa(0)=0">. Write <img src="assets/math/inline-0ecd48765e47be11.svg" width="12" height="18" alt="f"> for this fixed closed-loop field below. The subscript on <img src="assets/math/inline-3e507e9542909164.svg" width="19" height="18" alt="f_\kappa"> denotes a fixed controller and is independent of the scalar coupling strength used in Section 7.

Let <img src="assets/math/inline-347aa0cefed6cee0.svg" width="93" height="18" alt="\phi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^r"> be <img src="assets/math/inline-60c11d6fc4fa8a83.svg" width="24" height="17" alt="C^1"> and let <img src="assets/math/inline-b61df334ee04b6ac.svg" width="42" height="15" alt="\varepsilon&gt;0">. Define

**Equation (T1)**

<p align="center"><img src="assets/math/display-1d7e6d0771732259.svg" width="326" height="45" alt="V(x)=\varepsilon\|x\|^2+\|\phi(x)-\phi(0)\|^2."></p>

Every norm on a vector is Euclidean; every matrix norm is its induced 2-norm unless another norm is explicitly written. For radial Jacobian arguments, require <img src="assets/math/inline-2222643d25bcf240.svg" width="54" height="20" alt="f\in C^1"> on a neighborhood of each radial hull under consideration. The benchmark square is star shaped; for a general non-star-shaped <img src="assets/math/inline-2b08ffd953f7c889.svg" width="17" height="14" alt="D">, the field must also be defined on the portions of the radial hull outside <img src="assets/math/inline-2b08ffd953f7c889.svg" width="17" height="14" alt="D">.

## 2. Positive definiteness and regularity — manuscript Theorem 3

**Statement.** <img src="assets/math/inline-f6b3e82dc9a2938c.svg" width="58" height="17" alt="V\in C^1">, <img src="assets/math/inline-cf225cd71cb89c88.svg" width="68" height="19" alt="V(0)=0">, <img src="assets/math/inline-27bb378bd9529b87.svg" width="103" height="21" alt="V(x)\ge\varepsilon\|x\|^2">, and <img src="assets/math/inline-d398f815d679ed6c.svg" width="16" height="14" alt="V"> is radially unbounded.

**Proof.** A squared norm is a finite sum of squares of its components. Composition and finite sums of <img src="assets/math/inline-60c11d6fc4fa8a83.svg" width="24" height="17" alt="C^1"> functions remain <img src="assets/math/inline-60c11d6fc4fa8a83.svg" width="24" height="17" alt="C^1">. At the origin both terms in (T1) vanish. For <img src="assets/math/inline-249a703f8842d474.svg" width="43" height="18" alt="x\ne0">, the first term is positive and the second is nonnegative. Finally <img src="assets/math/inline-c70c03022882dec8.svg" width="147" height="21" alt="V(x)\ge\varepsilon\|x\|^2\to\infty"> as <img src="assets/math/inline-42acc6f536d1a7b7.svg" width="73" height="19" alt="\|x\|\to\infty">. ∎

Differentiating (T1) gives

**Equation (T2)**

<p align="center"><img src="assets/math/display-1c2b2216ae0502e5.svg" width="383" height="46" alt="\nabla V(x)=2\varepsilon x+2J_\phi(x)^\top[\phi(x)-\phi(0)]."></p>

## 3. Radial enclosure — manuscript Lemma 1

For an axis-aligned box <img src="assets/math/inline-3c811f549772a865.svg" width="72" height="19" alt="Q=[\ell,u]">, define

**Equation (T3)**

<p align="center"><img src="assets/math/display-a4ed746c27fd6140.svg" width="462" height="42" alt="R(Q)=\operatorname{hull}(\{0\}\cup Q)=[\min(0,\ell),\max(0,u)],"></p>

where the minimum and maximum act componentwise. For all <img src="assets/math/inline-c2a2404362024525.svg" width="46" height="18" alt="x\in Q"> and <img src="assets/math/inline-abfac5c79abfcda0.svg" width="63" height="19" alt="t\in[0,1]">, <img src="assets/math/inline-4354a3c79db1323a.svg" width="79" height="19" alt="tx\in R(Q)">. The fundamental theorem of calculus gives

**Equation (T4)**

<p align="center"><img src="assets/math/display-de60380f62c01151.svg" width="453" height="75" alt="\phi(x)-\phi(0)=B(x)x,\quad B(x)=\int_0^1J_\phi(tx)\,dt,"></p>

**Equation (T5)**

<p align="center"><img src="assets/math/display-9b44b841bceec4eb.svg" width="383" height="75" alt="f(x)=F(x)x,\quad F(x)=\int_0^1J_f(tx)\,dt."></p>

**Statement.** If interval matrices <img src="assets/math/inline-ba8a0c00ae9127a0.svg" width="75" height="20" alt="\mathcal J_\phi(R(Q))"> and <img src="assets/math/inline-eb99480ec9c8c19e.svg" width="75" height="20" alt="\mathcal J_f(R(Q))"> enclose the respective Jacobians everywhere on <img src="assets/math/inline-ef2dd6ef5059864a.svg" width="42" height="19" alt="R(Q)">, then they enclose <img src="assets/math/inline-6876c6dbaa5f2370.svg" width="38" height="19" alt="B(x)"> and <img src="assets/math/inline-e7ed118e57d1cf57.svg" width="38" height="19" alt="F(x)"> for every <img src="assets/math/inline-c2a2404362024525.svg" width="46" height="18" alt="x\in Q">. Sound interval operations applied to

**Equation (T6)**

<p align="center"><img src="assets/math/display-8891e23fbb936f55.svg" width="319" height="80" alt="\begin{aligned}
G(x)&amp;=2\varepsilon I+2J_\phi(x)^\top B(x),\\
H(x)&amp;=\operatorname{sym}\!\left(G(x)^\top F(x)\right)+cI.
\end{aligned}"></p>

also enclose <img src="assets/math/inline-3bb23bb0fee4a217.svg" width="39" height="19" alt="G(x)"> and <img src="assets/math/inline-5aabf6d9e30889f5.svg" width="41" height="19" alt="H(x)">. Here <img src="assets/math/inline-a7ab78bd592fc2b4.svg" width="174" height="21" alt="\operatorname{sym}M=(M+M^\top)/2"> and <img src="assets/math/inline-afd557a616c8e78c.svg" width="41" height="15" alt="c&gt;0">.

**Proof.** Fix an entry <img src="assets/math/inline-88e69f2d5abf6691.svg" width="23" height="17" alt="i,j">. Its value in (T4) is the integral average of a continuous scalar function whose entire range is in the interval <img src="assets/math/inline-e4bcc36d07a082bb.svg" width="57" height="20" alt="[a_{ij},b_{ij}]">. Integration of <img src="assets/math/inline-7b47db61ea0474da.svg" width="156" height="20" alt="a_{ij}\le (J_\phi(tx))_{ij}\le b_{ij}"> over an interval of length one preserves these inequalities. This proves entrywise inclusion of <img src="assets/math/inline-b0b59b83b5effd43.svg" width="15" height="14" alt="B">; the same argument proves inclusion of <img src="assets/math/inline-c3afc2dea66ccc19.svg" width="15" height="14" alt="F">. The endpoint Jacobian <img src="assets/math/inline-182b87c5d0a002b6.svg" width="43" height="20" alt="J_\phi(x)"> can be bounded on <img src="assets/math/inline-e48ccc68dcc31a3a.svg" width="16" height="18" alt="Q"> itself. Interval addition and multiplication that enclose their exact real results preserve these inclusions in (T6), even when dependency makes the result wider. ∎

For two tanh layers, <img src="assets/math/inline-4939205fc2ce688b.svg" width="158" height="19" alt="a_1=\tanh(W_1x+b_1)">, <img src="assets/math/inline-d58cef5f1f298a12.svg" width="158" height="19" alt="\phi=\tanh(W_2a_1+b_2)">,

**Equation (T7)**

<p align="center"><img src="assets/math/display-363a345c0489402e.svg" width="541" height="47" alt="J_\phi(x)=D_2(x)W_2D_1(x)W_1,\quad D_i=\operatorname{diag}(1-\tanh^2 z_i)."></p>

For the **main exported model**, the final activation is the identity, so <img src="assets/math/inline-267ab4b8aee27f0b.svg" width="55" height="17" alt="D_2=I">. The supplementary stress-test model uses both tanh layers. On a scalar interval <img src="assets/math/inline-b7952325dff06790.svg" width="36" height="19" alt="[a,b]">, <img src="assets/math/inline-f8b2abb4e2f1aaed.svg" width="37" height="14" alt="\tanh"> is monotone, and the minimum of <img src="assets/math/inline-0eae43d331f665cb.svg" width="41" height="18" alt="\operatorname{sech}^2"> occurs at the endpoint with largest absolute value. Its maximum is one if <img src="assets/math/inline-2731e9024446513d.svg" width="65" height="19" alt="0\in[a,b]">, otherwise it occurs at the endpoint closest to zero. All these endpoint evaluations require validated rounding when used in a machine proof.

## 4. Box-wise decrease — manuscript Theorem 2

Define the prescribed margin

**Equation (T8)**

<p align="center"><img src="assets/math/display-e0555d060179d136.svg" width="424" height="45" alt="m(x)=\nabla V(x)^\top f(x)+c\|x\|^2=x^\top H(x)x."></p>

**Statement.** Suppose a sound interval matrix encloses <img src="assets/math/inline-5aabf6d9e30889f5.svg" width="41" height="19" alt="H(x)"> for every <img src="assets/math/inline-c2a2404362024525.svg" width="46" height="18" alt="x\in Q"> and a sound scalar upper bound satisfies <img src="assets/math/inline-b1ea005abdcc6fe0.svg" width="162" height="23" alt="\lambda_{\max}(H(x))\le\bar\lambda_Q&lt;0"> throughout <img src="assets/math/inline-e48ccc68dcc31a3a.svg" width="16" height="18" alt="Q">. Then

**Equation (T9)**

<p align="center"><img src="assets/math/display-9a95b0ff8f810f9d.svg" width="269" height="48" alt="\dot V(x)\le-c\|x\|^2\quad(x\in Q),"></p>

with a strictly negative margin for every nonzero <img src="assets/math/inline-596a938169557684.svg" width="12" height="10" alt="x">.

**Proof.** From (T2), (T4), and (T6), <img src="assets/math/inline-372cb250f291bfa1.svg" width="75" height="16" alt="\nabla V=Gx">; from (T5), <img src="assets/math/inline-e7b10868ec0aab77.svg" width="57" height="18" alt="f=Fx">. The quadratic form of a skew-symmetric matrix is zero, so (T8) follows. The Rayleigh quotient for the symmetric matrix <img src="assets/math/inline-92cc7ae4a438b8d1.svg" width="18" height="14" alt="H"> yields <img src="assets/math/inline-c8c8d8606baae8e8.svg" width="149" height="23" alt="m(x)\le\bar\lambda_Q\|x\|^2&lt;0"> for <img src="assets/math/inline-249a703f8842d474.svg" width="43" height="18" alt="x\ne0">. At zero both sides of (T9) are zero. Subtracting <img src="assets/math/inline-ea8e6d6411afce93.svg" width="44" height="21" alt="c\|x\|^2"> proves the result. ∎

For a symmetric interval matrix with diagonal upper endpoints <img src="assets/math/inline-f77fe2c4780cba12.svg" width="22" height="21" alt="\bar h_{ii}"> and off-diagonal ranges <img src="assets/math/inline-2b30cfa87891387e.svg" width="60" height="27" alt="[\underline h_{ij},\bar h_{ij}]">, Gershgorin gives

**Equation (T10)**

<p align="center"><img src="assets/math/display-9aa7cb9c2629dbd3.svg" width="395" height="89" alt="\bar\lambda_Q=\max_i\left(\bar h_{ii}+\sum_{j\ne i}\max(|\underline h_{ij}|,|\bar h_{ij}|)\right)."></p>

The maximum and the sums must also be bounded outward. A finite partition covering <img src="assets/math/inline-2b08ffd953f7c889.svg" width="17" height="14" alt="D"> proves (T9) on <img src="assets/math/inline-2b08ffd953f7c889.svg" width="17" height="14" alt="D"> if every leaf is discharged soundly. Away from zero, a direct interval evaluation with <img src="assets/math/inline-8058bde71622cdf8.svg" width="104" height="19" alt="\sup m(Q)\le0"> also suffices. A finite grid or partition geometry alone does not prove the inequality.

### Benchmark-specific factorization and the general Jacobian

For <img src="assets/math/inline-dd9acbc0281a1098.svg" width="173" height="19" alt="f(x)=Ax+0.6x_1JPx">, the archived verifier uses the exact factorization

**Equation (T11)**

<p align="center"><img src="assets/math/display-07bcc623c12aa79d.svg" width="449" height="44" alt="F_{\rm alg}(x)=A+0.6x_1JP,\qquad f(x)=F_{\rm alg}(x)x."></p>

This is sufficient for (T8) and avoids a looser enclosure. It need not equal the radial integral in (T5). The actual vector-field Jacobian is

**Equation (T12)**

<p align="center"><img src="assets/math/display-cb90852f009fe96e.svg" width="356" height="46" alt="J_f(x)=A+0.6[(JPx)e_1^\top+x_1JP],"></p>

and its radial integral is <img src="assets/math/inline-2c91f474c6254f83.svg" width="194" height="22" alt="A+0.3[(JPx)e_1^\top+x_1JP]">. Multiplication of either factor by <img src="assets/math/inline-596a938169557684.svg" width="12" height="10" alt="x"> gives the same <img src="assets/math/inline-2566b5e949a84a53.svg" width="35" height="19" alt="f(x)">. In a general application, (T11) must not be substituted for the Jacobian; the omitted product-rule term matters.

### Quadratic upper and gradient bounds

If <img src="assets/math/inline-2497d76be435ca93.svg" width="88" height="19" alt="\|B(x)\|\le\beta"> and <img src="assets/math/inline-7a7d8ff02ccef9c4.svg" width="87" height="19" alt="\|G(x)\|\le g"> on <img src="assets/math/inline-2b08ffd953f7c889.svg" width="17" height="14" alt="D">, then

**Equation (T13)**

<p align="center"><img src="assets/math/display-702b6a071e974eca.svg" width="348" height="74" alt="\begin{aligned}
V(x)&amp;\le b\|x\|^2,\qquad b=\varepsilon+\beta^2,\\
\|\nabla V(x)\|&amp;\le g\|x\|.
\end{aligned}"></p>

The first inequality follows by (T1) and (T4); the second follows from <img src="assets/math/inline-372cb250f291bfa1.svg" width="75" height="16" alt="\nabla V=Gx">. A matrix interval <img src="assets/math/inline-e2a1e5bf3a76baab.svg" width="44" height="19" alt="[L,U]"> admits the conservative norm bound <img src="assets/math/inline-ab38eb6e0a58c014.svg" width="170" height="24" alt="\|M\|_2\le\sqrt{\|K\|_1\|K\|_\infty}"> with <img src="assets/math/inline-822c7097cfd5bb33.svg" width="166" height="20" alt="K_{ij}=\max(|L_{ij}|,|U_{ij}|)">. These computations require sound arithmetic if their outputs support a proof.

## 5. Invariant sublevel and exponential estimate — manuscript Corollary 1

**Statement.** Suppose on <img src="assets/math/inline-2b08ffd953f7c889.svg" width="17" height="14" alt="D">

**Equation (T14)**

<p align="center"><img src="assets/math/display-3bef6c0d479c0bce.svg" width="441" height="48" alt="\varepsilon\|x\|^2\le V(x)\le b\|x\|^2,\qquad
\dot V(x)\le-c\|x\|^2,"></p>

where <img src="assets/math/inline-9f6653736e8c9a91.svg" width="56" height="18" alt="b,c&gt;0">. Let <img src="assets/math/inline-a32f15ce2fc9b346.svg" width="42" height="17" alt="\rho&gt;0"> and let the complete sublevel <img src="assets/math/inline-a7f5baceefa213d9.svg" width="153" height="20" alt="\Omega_\rho=\{x:V(x)\le\rho\}"> be contained in <img src="assets/math/inline-66dcbaf3bcfbf31c.svg" width="40" height="14" alt="\operatorname{int}D">. Every solution with <img src="assets/math/inline-6cc8581e388f11c5.svg" width="75" height="20" alt="x(0)\in\Omega_\rho"> exists for all <img src="assets/math/inline-e24ca25e7f937e15.svg" width="40" height="16" alt="t\ge0">, remains there, and satisfies

**Equation (T15)**

<p align="center"><img src="assets/math/display-cffce66f9b020305.svg" width="306" height="61" alt="\|x(t)\|\le\sqrt{b/\varepsilon}\,e^{-ct/(2b)}\|x(0)\|."></p>

**Proof.** The sublevel is closed and bounded by (T1), hence compact. On its boundary <img src="assets/math/inline-4b1ab240076f6334.svg" width="78" height="18" alt="V=\rho&gt;0">, so <img src="assets/math/inline-249a703f8842d474.svg" width="43" height="18" alt="x\ne0"> and <img src="assets/math/inline-6c7de8a901d86bbe.svg" width="47" height="20" alt="\dot V&lt;0">. A trajectory cannot exit to a larger value of <img src="assets/math/inline-d398f815d679ed6c.svg" width="16" height="14" alt="V">. More explicitly, integrating the differential inequality up to a first possible exit gives <img src="assets/math/inline-315ed4124bb128be.svg" width="92" height="19" alt="V(t)\le V(0)">; a boundary trajectory immediately decreases, which rules out that exit. The solution therefore stays in a compact subset of the open existence domain. Local Lipschitz continuity and the standard continuation theorem preclude finite-time termination there. Since <img src="assets/math/inline-27d4262a2106d990.svg" width="80" height="21" alt="V\le b\|x\|^2">, <img src="assets/math/inline-3bddd7f60fb84c5f.svg" width="101" height="24" alt="\dot V\le-(c/b)V">. Integrating gives <img src="assets/math/inline-fe0b00ef62436e7a.svg" width="178" height="22" alt="V(x(t))\le V(x(0))e^{-ct/b}">. Apply the lower bound at <img src="assets/math/inline-5db5238d4ff87096.svg" width="9" height="13" alt="t"> and the upper bound at zero and take square roots. ∎

For <img src="assets/math/inline-86f092ce9681699e.svg" width="94" height="21" alt="D=[-2,2]^2"> and <img src="assets/math/inline-b137455091df06d1.svg" width="63" height="15" alt="\varepsilon=0.02">, every point on or outside its boundary has <img src="assets/math/inline-bc6d0e75e92e9401.svg" width="68" height="16" alt="V\ge0.08">. Thus <img src="assets/math/inline-cec0875e87104f32.svg" width="98" height="17" alt="\Omega_{0.04}\subset\operatorname{int}D"> follows **architecturally**. Invariance additionally requires the derivative inequality on that set; the numerical guarded calculation does not by itself prove it.

## 6. Structured robustness — manuscript Proposition 1

**Statement.** Assume (T14), <img src="assets/math/inline-10dc9e38d6a4bb38.svg" width="127" height="19" alt="\|\nabla V(x)\|\le g\|x\|"> on <img src="assets/math/inline-2b08ffd953f7c889.svg" width="17" height="14" alt="D">, and a locally Lipschitz perturbed field

**Equation (T16)**

<p align="center"><img src="assets/math/display-f239b972d4ba04c2.svg" width="483" height="42" alt="f_{\rm true}(x)=f(x)+\delta Bx,\qquad
c_\delta=c-|\delta|g\|B\|&gt;0."></p>

For a complete sublevel <img src="assets/math/inline-28a4be633e32498c.svg" width="83" height="20" alt="\Omega_\rho\subset\operatorname{int}D">, the perturbed system is forward invariant there and

**Equation (T17)**

<p align="center"><img src="assets/math/display-08524e5ac267ddfc.svg" width="312" height="61" alt="\|x(t)\|\le\sqrt{b/\varepsilon}\,e^{-c_\delta t/(2b)}\|x(0)\|."></p>

**Proof.** Cauchy–Schwarz and the induced matrix norm give

<p align="center"><img src="assets/math/display-0511f7626acb8c0c.svg" width="413" height="111" alt="\begin{aligned}
\dot V_{\rm true}(x)
&amp;=\nabla V(x)^\top f(x)+\delta\nabla V(x)^\top Bx\\
&amp;\le-c\|x\|^2+|\delta|\,\|\nabla V(x)\|\,\|B\|\,\|x\|\\
&amp;\le-c_\delta\|x\|^2.
\end{aligned}"></p>

The preceding invariance, continuation, and comparison proof applies with <img src="assets/math/inline-2d0014b7593c56cb.svg" width="17" height="13" alt="c_\delta"> in place of <img src="assets/math/inline-ad441576e8ea267e.svg" width="10" height="10" alt="c">. ∎

The manuscript treats <img src="assets/math/inline-2bf63149de0f4c4a.svg" width="10" height="15" alt="\delta"> as a nonnegative perturbation magnitude. The absolute value in (T16) explicitly extends that convention to signed <img src="assets/math/inline-2bf63149de0f4c4a.svg" width="10" height="15" alt="\delta">. More generally <img src="assets/math/inline-d552fb867bfbbe30.svg" width="111" height="19" alt="\|d(x)\|\le\mu\|x\|"> gives the reduced coefficient <img src="assets/math/inline-0cb1f3480917dcb3.svg" width="49" height="16" alt="c-g\mu"> under the same existence assumptions.

## 7. Two coupled subsystems — manuscript Proposition 2

**Statement.** Suppose (T14) and the gradient bound hold on <img src="assets/math/inline-2b08ffd953f7c889.svg" width="17" height="14" alt="D">. Consider

If <img src="assets/math/inline-af7e9e8110f164d4.svg" width="90" height="19" alt="|\kappa|&lt;c/(2g)"> and <img src="assets/math/inline-5936624c021d65bb.svg" width="283" height="20" alt="S_\rho=\{(z_1,z_2):V_\Sigma\le\rho\}\subset\operatorname{int}(D\times D)">, this sublevel is forward invariant and, for <img src="assets/math/inline-3ea1ccf8e663b507.svg" width="85" height="19" alt="z=(z_1,z_2)">,

<p align="center"><img src="assets/math/display-0b9e07e3bd6bae91.svg" width="310" height="61" alt="\|z(t)\|\le\sqrt{b/\varepsilon}\,e^{-c_\Sigma t/(2b)}\|z(0)\|."></p>

**Proof.** Set <img src="assets/math/inline-ef679c497cbee301.svg" width="66" height="19" alt="a=\|z_1\|">, <img src="assets/math/inline-07b5642ecd0264c7.svg" width="66" height="19" alt="d=\|z_2\|">. The isolated terms sum to at most <img src="assets/math/inline-45c2f3eb4cf0b6b5.svg" width="90" height="21" alt="-c(a^2+d^2)">. By the gradient bound and triangle inequality, the two coupling terms sum to at most

<p align="center"><img src="assets/math/display-4d609bf2bce311fa.svg" width="562" height="45" alt="|\kappa|g[a(a+d)+d(d+a)]
=|\kappa|g(a+d)^2\le2|\kappa|g(a^2+d^2)."></p>

This proves (T19). Sum the two quadratic bounds in (T14), and apply the proof of Section 5 to the joint state and <img src="assets/math/inline-9a7830b17c8917b5.svg" width="51" height="16" alt="c_\Sigma&gt;0">. ∎

This is a sufficient bound for two identical diffusively coupled systems, not a general graph or ISS small-gain theorem. For the benchmark, the same floor implies <img src="assets/math/inline-0d42acfb9f25574a.svg" width="141" height="19" alt="S_{0.04}\subset\operatorname{int}(D\times D)">.

## 8. Independent analytical benchmark identities

### Calibration system

**Equation (T21)**

<p align="center"><img src="assets/math/display-2de18d7b7d02b631.svg" width="516" height="86" alt="A=\begin{bmatrix}-1&amp;4\\-\frac{1}{2}&amp;-1\end{bmatrix},\quad
P=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{17}{48}&amp;\frac{7}{24}\\\frac{7}{24}&amp;\frac{5}{3}\end{bmatrix},\quad
J=\begin{bmatrix}0&amp;-1\\1&amp;0\end{bmatrix}."></p>

Direct multiplication gives <img src="assets/math/inline-207c7d7928a53c86.svg" width="130" height="18" alt="A^\top P+PA=-I">. The leading minor <img src="assets/math/inline-42e05c247060f32b.svg" width="76" height="19" alt="17/48&gt;0"> and determinant <img src="assets/math/inline-20189cc0b8155e1f.svg" width="85" height="19" alt="97/192&gt;0"> show <img src="assets/math/inline-623f9cf08e89819b.svg" width="46" height="15" alt="P\succ0">. For <img src="assets/math/inline-3895b6a94f9b093d.svg" width="94" height="19" alt="V_{\rm ref}=x^\top Px"> and the field in (T11),

**Equation (T22)**

<p align="center"><img src="assets/math/display-1e3a9cd878309b7f.svg" width="541" height="48" alt="\dot V_{\rm ref}=x^\top(A^\top P+PA)x+1.2x_1(Px)^\top J(Px)=-\|x\|^2."></p>

The last term vanishes because <img src="assets/math/inline-4d7bffd540d06b1e.svg" width="72" height="18" alt="J^\top=-J">. This is a global analytical certificate and is stronger than sampled evidence for a learned candidate.

### Non-polynomial reference

For <img src="assets/math/inline-42b04d33737d7a84.svg" width="128" height="18" alt="\dot x_1=-x_1+x_1x_2">, <img src="assets/math/inline-fe779196da735318.svg" width="73" height="18" alt="\dot x_2=-x_2">, define

**Equation (T23)**

<p align="center"><img src="assets/math/display-abdb872ef201828b.svg" width="275" height="46" alt="V_{\log}(x)=\log(1+x_1^2)+x_2^2."></p>

It is positive definite, smooth, and radially unbounded. Differentiation and completion of squares yield

**Equation (T24)**

<p align="center"><img src="assets/math/display-bedd37a1e6a00dc0.svg" width="550" height="79" alt="\dot V_{\log}=
-\frac{x_1^2+2x_2^2+x_1^2x_2^2+(x_1-x_1x_2)^2}{1+x_1^2}&lt;0\quad(x\ne0)."></p>

All terms in the numerator are nonnegative, and <img src="assets/math/inline-ec1caa4f99db4650.svg" width="97" height="22" alt="x_1^2+2x_2^2&gt;0"> off the origin. Proper sublevels and the same continuation argument give global asymptotic stability. The claim that this polynomial vector field admits no global polynomial Lyapunov function is a cited result, not proved here: Ahmadi, Krstic, and Parrilo, CDC 2011, [doi:10.1109/CDC.2011.6161499](https://doi.org/10.1109/CDC.2011.6161499). A compact-domain neural experiment does not itself establish that global obstruction.

## 9. Numerical event and binomial bound

Fix the selected network before generating the test sample. Let <img src="assets/math/inline-d911c949a914ee99.svg" width="22" height="17" alt="X_i"> be IID uniform on <img src="assets/math/inline-2b08ffd953f7c889.svg" width="17" height="14" alt="D"> and define

**Equation (T25)**

<p align="center"><img src="assets/math/display-952fe2dd08acbb4c.svg" width="397" height="45" alt="E_\tau=\{x:\|x\|^2&gt;10^{-8},\ m(x)&gt;10^{-10}\}."></p>

The numerical implementation, precision, and tolerances are part of the experiment. The deterministic grid is excluded from the binomial trial count. If <img src="assets/math/inline-2812b5cbd3286187.svg" width="85" height="19" alt="p=\Pr(E_\tau)">, independence gives <img src="assets/math/inline-8bb7e521cff51a78.svg" width="239" height="21" alt="\Pr(\text{zero events in }N)=(1-p)^N">. Inverting this probability at <img src="assets/math/inline-2923151d7a110374.svg" width="75" height="17" alt="\alpha=1-\gamma"> gives the exact one-sided zero-event Clopper–Pearson upper confidence endpoint

**Equation (T26)**

<p align="center"><img src="assets/math/display-140173a5bef14042.svg" width="164" height="46" alt="p_U=1-\alpha^{1/N}."></p>

At <img src="assets/math/inline-f267ebb09bc5c5b9.svg" width="91" height="16" alt="N=200000">, <img src="assets/math/inline-d640fad7a27cfbd8.svg" width="65" height="17" alt="\gamma=0.95">, <img src="assets/math/inline-1f99db4a8d2b07ea.svg" width="172" height="20" alt="p_U\simeq1.4978549\times10^{-5}">. This is a repeated-sampling confidence statement about the declared numerical event under this distribution. It does not bound the exact event <img src="assets/math/inline-a387eaa2c22ade02.svg" width="72" height="19" alt="m(x)&gt;0">, does not transfer automatically to another distribution, and does not imply continuum verification. With nonzero event counts, the zero-event formula must not be used.

## 10. Hard and soft CLF filters

For control-affine <img src="assets/math/inline-7abaa848350e4c8d.svg" width="143" height="20" alt="\dot x=f_0(x)+g_0(x)u">, the hard filter minimizes <img src="assets/math/inline-c38687ef74815531.svg" width="110" height="21" alt="\|u-u_{\rm NN}(x)\|^2"> over <img src="assets/math/inline-081f915b841c36c2.svg" width="46" height="15" alt="u\in U"> subject to <img src="assets/math/inline-cd2c4ba511a49121.svg" width="194" height="21" alt="\nabla V^\top(f_0+g_0u)\le-c\|x\|^2">. If feasible throughout the operating set and the resulting dynamics admit solutions to which the derivative inequality applies, the same comparison proof establishes decay.

The soft filter adds <img src="assets/math/inline-c83429c00c7f4451.svg" width="42" height="16" alt="s\ge0">, a penalty <img src="assets/math/inline-9bfb89df113a2c53.svg" width="26" height="20" alt="p s^2">, and allows <img src="assets/math/inline-f30f5ae089ecf36b.svg" width="223" height="21" alt="\nabla V^\top(f_0+g_0u)\le-c\|x\|^2+s">. Positive slack by itself does not imply strict decrease: it only gives the stated upper bound. A further bound such as <img src="assets/math/inline-59c2482e819cc43f.svg" width="100" height="21" alt="s(x)\le\sigma\|x\|^2"> with <img src="assets/math/inline-3b7e90f2c6f47313.svg" width="42" height="12" alt="\sigma&lt;c"> would recover a reduced rate. Neither filter's numerical implementation is part of the supplied benchmark experiments; they are control-use formulations.
